scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Tango Liso emerged in Buenos Aires between 1905 and 1910 as the dance migrated from the outskirts to central dance halls.
These venues were often small and catered to Italian immigrants who lacked the training for more complex, aggressive styles.
The style was further refined by professional dancers in Italian dance academies, eventually evolving into ballroom tango and influencing the development of Tango de Salon.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Tango Liso served as a democratic form of social expression, accessible to those who could not master the demanding 'cortes y quebradas.' It represented a shift toward a more 'cultured' and Europeanized social dance.
Its meaning is tied to the immigrant experience in Buenos Aires and the eventual global validation of Argentine culture through the lens of Parisian high society.
Today it is a historical tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance is characterized by a smooth, simplified choreography that prioritizes walking steps (caminada).
Dancers maintain a vertical torso and keep their feet flush to the ground, avoiding the heel-stamping of earlier styles.
The movement involves a cycle between close and open embrace, with the couple remaining offset to their right.
Watch for Caminada, Ochos.

Formation: Couples remain offset to their right; movement is often rotary to accommodate crowded dance floors.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: During the formative years of Tango Liso, the music underwent an 'Italization.' This included the short-lived use of instruments such as the mandolin and accordion in primitive tango bands.
The music moved away from the complex African rhythms of earlier tango to support the more predictable and smooth movements of the Liso style.
Listen for the Mandolin, Accordion, Guitar, Violin.
The pulse is 4/4.

A softer, more melodic version of early tango that incorporated Italian instruments like the mandolin. It lacks the sharp, aggressive accents of the 'cortes y quebradas' era, favoring a smoother, more flowing auditory experience.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: The dance was born in the 'arrabales' (outskirt districts) and moved into small, centrally located dance halls in Buenos Aires.
These settings were often over-crowded, which dictated the compact, rotary nature of the dance.
The atmosphere was more 'genteel' than the earlier rowdy settings, reflecting the aspirations of the Italian immigrant clientele who frequented these academies.

scenes.title: The people
narration: The sources mention that professional dancers working in Italian dance halls and academies were responsible for refining the style, though individual names are not specified.
It is noted that traditional tangueros of the era initially despised the style for its simplicity.
The primary variants identified are the original Tango Liso of Buenos Aires and the 'Tango Liso Paris' version.
Tango Liso is a subclass of Tango.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Tango Liso is parent of Ballroom Tango: Tango Liso's codification in instruction books helped establish the basic techniques of ballroom tango.
Tango Liso is sibling of Tango de Salon: Tango de Salon is an offshoot that reintroduced some of the intensity removed by Liso.
